subject: EchoMeds dedicated commit: metering, SLO fit and GPU allocation playbook
messages:
From: Sarah Lin <sarah@echomeds.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>
Cc: procure@echomeds.com
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 09:17:00 -0700
Subject: Capacity and SLO alignment for EchoMeds dedicated commit

Hi Naomi,

Thanks again for the demo last week. EchoMeds is budgeting for a dedicated commit to run our primary clinical summarization model (approx. 1.2B parameters) behind our API. Procurement asked me to put the expected throughput and SLOs in writing so we can model costs and confirm the statement of work. Key asks from our side: 

- Expected sustainable tokens/sec for mixed traffic (inference + few-shot prompting) with a 95th percentile latency SLO of ~200ms per call (our calls average 120 tokens).
- Recommended GPU SKUs and slab sizing (preferred: minimal oversubscription, but we need cost predictability).
- Required headroom (% buffer) you recommend for launch and for 6-week ramp.
- Any fallback/quantization variant we should enumerate for the contract.

Attached is a 24h sample of our request traces (EchoMeds_workload_sample.csv). We can be flexible on exact SLA wording if the performance targets require a variant-based fallback.

Can you and your eng lead provide a short metering playbook and a recommended slab commitment we can attach to the SOW? Procurement is hoping to close preliminary terms this week.

Thanks,
Sarah
Sarah Lin
Head of ML Ops, EchoMeds
Attachments: EchoMeds_workload_sample.csv
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Lin <sarah@echomeds.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 11:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Capacity and SLO alignment for EchoMeds dedicated commit

Sarah —

Appreciate the sample trace. I pulled a few quick stats from the CSV and sketched an initial playbook below. This is conservative but pragmatic for a committed slab + short ramp: 

Summary (initial assumptions)
- Median request size: ~120 tokens per call (matches your note).
- Measured avg tokens/sec from sample (burst-aware): ~720 t/s sustained, peaks ~1,800 t/s over short windows.
- Target p95 latency SLO: 200ms per call.

Redwood recommendation (first-pass)
1) Baseline throughput estimate: 1,000 tokens/sec reserved for the slab to cover steady-state + short bursts with graceful queuing. This maps to approx 8k calls/min at 120 tokens/call.
2) GPU SKU mapping: We recommend mixing 1x A100-80GB-equivalent slab nodes for the primary serving (model weights + KV cache) at a ratio of ~1 node per 2500-3000 tokens/sec for this 1.2B model when using fp16 execution paths. For quantized variants (int8/4), per-GPU throughput improves ~1.8x-2.5x depending on kernel availability.
3) Reserved slab sizing: start with a 1.5x safety factor on top of baseline => commit target: 1,500 tokens/sec equivalent. Operationally this equates to 1 slab of 3 GPUs (3 x A100-80GB-equivalent) in our sizing graph for predictable throughput and to allow for one-GPU maintenance replacement without dropping below committed throughput.
4) Headroom policy: 20% headroom for launch (short term) then reevaluate at week 6. If adoption matches the sample, reduce to 10% or scale slab horizontally.
5) Canary/fallback: Ship with a canary route that falls back to an int8-quantized variant when measured p95 hits 220ms. That fallback should be automatic in the first 2 months of production.

Risks and tradeoffs
- Using aggressive quantization reduces latency and tokens/sec costs but may introduce slight regression in clinical phrasing. We recommend running your eval set against proposed quant variants before allowing automatic fallback.
- The 3-GPU slab keeps billing predictable but has lower burst-to-peak headroom than a larger distributed slab. It's a tradeoff between cost visibility and peak absorption.

Next steps (for procurement/SOW)
- I can produce a short SLA appendix that lists the committed tokens/sec, supported model variant(s), automatic fallback thresholds, and maintenance windows.
- Ben and Kim will follow up with GPU SKU mapping and billing footnotes (e.g., reserved billing cadence, burst credits).

If you want, we can hop on a 30-minute call tomorrow to finalize numbers before procurement drafts the SOW.

—Naomi
Naomi Feldman
Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwood.com>, Sarah Lin <sarah@echomeds.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 09:13:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Capacity and SLO alignment for EchoMeds dedicated commit

Adding a couple of implementation specifics to Naomi's excellent summary.

Throughput per GPU (empirical):
- A100-80GB-equivalent (fp16): ~900-1,100 t/s for 1.2B model depending on kv-cache hit and request length distribution.
- A100-80GB-equivalent (int8 fast kernels): ~1,700-2,300 t/s if optimized kernels available.

Given Naomi's baseline of 1,000 t/s: you can choose either:
A) 3x A100 fp16 nodes => nominal aggregate 2,700-3,300 t/s with some multi-tenant overhead; commit 1 slab (3 GPUs) as Naomi suggested (conservative billing).
B) 2x A100 fp16 + automatic int8 fallback => gives lower steady billing but requires a tested quantized release. If you want predictable p95 on call, option A with the 3-GPU slab is safer.

Operational notes:
- Warmup: plan a KV warmup phase on rollout; we recommend a short traffic seeding window (2–4 hours of gradual ramp) so cache efficiency reaches expected levels.
- Autoscaling/burst credits: we can provide a limited burst pool (metered) for short peaks above committed slab at a premium rate. That sits behind a credit contract you can accept in the SOW.

I'll prepare a one-page GPU mapping to include in the SOW (SKU names, per-GPU throughput ranges, billing footnotes).

—Ben
Principal Capacity Architect, Redwood Inference
